issues.legal_issue: A non-statutory administrative direction cannot by itself authorize the displacement of trustees from property held for the purposes of an institution.
material_facts: The pleadings that the managing committee had purchased the school land and built the school building on it were not specifically denied.
The Court proceeded on the basis that the committee held the land and building as trustees for the purposes of the school, not as beneficial owners.
The education code provision relied on to displace the committee was issued under the Director of Public Instruction’s authority and had no greater force than an administrative order.
issues.conclusion: The administrative provision did not have the force of law and could not authorize deprivation of the committee’s rights in the land and building.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(1) of the Constitution requires deprivation of property to be by authority of law. The Court considered Article 13 in determining whether the amended provision was law and concluded, on the stated preface to the Education Code and the concession for the respondents, that it was only an administrative order. The Court did not rely on an earlier case to decide this issue.

predicates.constitutional_property_claim: A claimant brings a constitutional proceeding alleging interference with a property right.
predicates.property_held_as_trustee: An institution’s land or buildings are held by its managing body as trustee for the institution’s purposes.
predicates.governing_direction_only_administrative: The direction relied on to displace the holder was issued only as an administrative order and had no statutory or other legal force.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property claim concerns property held for an institution by trustees and the direction relied on is only administrative, that direction cannot authorize deprivation of the property.

issues.legal_issue: A demonstrated threat to take control of property without lawful authority warrants constitutional relief against interference with that property.
material_facts: The managing committee held the school land and building as trustees for the school’s purposes.
Government officers formed an ad hoc committee and demanded that the existing committee hand over charge of the school.
An official communication directed officers to obtain help from local executive authorities if necessary to implement the takeover.
The respondents had no legal authority, apart from the administrative provision, to deprive the committee of its rights in the property.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the petition and prohibited the respondents from interfering with the petitioners’ property except by authority of law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy where a fundamental right is actually infringed or threatened with infringement. Read with Article 31(1), property cannot be taken without authority of law. The official communication authorizing recourse to local executive assistance showed that the apprehended dispossession was not merely imaginary. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: constitutional_property_proceeding and property_held_as_trustee and threatened_forced_takeover and no_lawful_authority_for_takeover

predicates.constitutional_property_proceeding: A claimant brings a constitutional proceeding seeking protection of a property right.
predicates.property_held_as_trustee: A managing body holds an institution’s property as trustee for the institution’s purposes.
predicates.threatened_forced_takeover: Officials demand transfer of control and are authorized to seek executive assistance to carry it out.
predicates.no_lawful_authority_for_takeover: The officials have no legal authority for the proposed takeover.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property proceeding concerns property held in trust and officials threaten a takeover without lawful authority, the court prohibits interference unless it is lawfully authorized.
